J1_line_asserts_challenged_proposition.justification: The response challenges "any walk between two vertices in a tree must be a path because the tree is circuit-free." First-choice line 7 is "3. By def., tree is circuit-free, so P_1 is a path (since path has no repeated edges and no repeated vertices)". The only thing in force about P_1 is line 6, "By def., tree is connected, so, there is a walk P_1 between u and v": P_1 is an arbitrary witness of connectedness, with no minimality or simplicity assumed, and T is a tree (line 5). So the inference line 7 states has to hold for an arbitrary u-v walk, which is exactly the challenged proposition; the source also supplies its own definition of path there (no repeated edges, no repeated vertices).

J2_evidence_specified.justification: A concrete tree and a concrete walk: "In the tree consisting of the edges u-x and x-v, the walk u-x-u-x-v connects u to v but repeats vertex x and the edge u-x, yet contains no circuit (no closed trail), showing the claim is false." Graph, walk, the repetitions and the circuit-freeness are all stated.

J3_evidence_check.justification: Exact finite check of the supplied witness, script kept. The graph on {u,x,v} with edges ux and xv is connected with |E| = |V|-1, hence a tree, and an exhaustive search finds no closed walk of positive length without a repeated edge (up to length 6, which exceeds anything possible on two edges), so it is circuit-free under the closed-trail reading of 'circuit' -- and a fortiori under the stricter 'cycle' reading. The walk u-x-u-x-v has every consecutive pair an edge, so it is a genuine u-v walk of the kind line 6 produces, and it repeats both the vertex x (and u) and the edge ux, so by the source's own definition quoted in line 7 it is not a path. Hence the assumptions in force at line 7 (T a tree, P_1 some u-v walk) are satisfied while the asserted conclusion fails: line 7's inference is refuted as written. The script also confirms the witness tree has exactly one simple u-v path, so the counterexample hits the inference and not the theorem.

J4_consequence_overreach.justification: The final saved answer is only the JSON object with one label, the challenged claim and the counterexample; it draws no consequence beyond that line. In particular it never suggests the theorem being proved (a unique path between distinct vertices of a tree) is false, and the deliberations it records about other lines are not asserted as consequences.

notes: One interpretive dependency for the adjudicator: the refutation requires reading P_1 as an arbitrary walk supplied by connectedness, which is what lines 6-7 literally give. A charitable reader could instead take the author to be choosing a convenient walk (e.g. a shortest one), under which line 7 becomes defensible; under the 'false as written' framing the response's reading is the right one. The definition of 'circuit' matters too, and the witness survives both standard choices (closed trail or cycle) -- under the untenable reading where any closed walk counts as a circuit, no graph with an edge would be circuit-free at all. The response's own deliberations wobble (it first writes 'So line 7 might be okay' before settling on 7) and it also identifies line 10 as false; I graded only the first-choice line and the final claim and witness.
